c.tagline: Ecuador's steamy Pacific port, riverfront Malecón, and gateway to the Galápagos.

taxi.fareNote: Many street taxis do not run the meter for tourists; agree the fare before getting in, or use Uber/InDrive/Cabify for a set price and added safety. Official airport taxis use fixed zone pricing paid at a counter (about $5-8 to downtown).

emergency.note: ECU 911 is Ecuador's single nationwide emergency line connecting police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Avoid south of Portete de Tarqui Ave, El Guasmo and northern suburbs (Kennedy/Alborada).
Muggings even on the Malecón — stay in Samborondón/Puerto Santa Ana.

hood_desc: The central downtown core along the Malecón 2000 riverfront promenade, lined with gardens, museums, an IMAX, malls, and restaurants overlooking the Guayas River; the most convenient, walkable base for first-timers who want the main sights on their doorstep.

Guayaquil's oldest neighborhood and a declared Cultural Heritage site, a colorful hillside of restored 400-year-old colonial houses, art galleries, and cafes climbing the 444 steps of Cerro Santa Ana to a lighthouse with sweeping river views; best for travelers into history and photography.

A leafy middle-class district west of downtown famous for its dining and nightlife, with Victor Emilio Estrada avenue packed with restaurants, bars, cafes, and shops serving everything from ceviche to sushi; a more local, going-out vibe.

An upscale, master-planned residential enclave across the river in La Puntilla, synonymous with luxury: gated communities, high-end malls, riverside restaurants, and modern towers; calm, secure, and car-dependent, favored by affluent locals and long-stay visitors.

A modern redeveloped waterfront district just north of Las Peñas, with a marina, riverside boardwalk, sleek residential towers, hotels, bars, restaurants, and a music museum; a polished, safe-feeling riverfront pocket good for dining and evenings out.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water, as most residents do.

transit.hours: The Metrovía and Aerovía generally run from around 5:00/6:00 AM to about 10:00/11:00 PM daily; there is no late-night service, so ride-hailing apps or taxis cover the overnight hours.
transit.note: Guayaquil has no underground metro; the backbone is the Metrovía bus rapid transit network (three trunk corridors on dedicated lanes with feeder buses), complemented by the Aerovía aerial cable car linking downtown to Durán. Petty theft on crowded buses is common, so keep valuables secure.
transit.pay: The Metrovía BRT charges a flat $0.45 (reduced $0.15 for students/seniors), paid in cash at station turnstiles or with the reloadable 'La Guayaca' card; the Aerovía cable car across the Guayas River to Durán is $0.76. Ordinary city buses are paid in cash (about $0.35) directly to the driver.

air: José Joaquín de Olmedo International Airport (GYE)
bus: Terminal Terrestre Jaime Roldós Aguilera (main intercity bus terminal, next to the airport)
ferry: Port of Guayaquil (Puerto Marítimo, cargo); river ferries across the Guayas
train: Tren Ecuador heritage tourist services from Durán (Tren de la Costa, subject to operation)

airport.name: José Joaquín de Olmedo International Airport (GYE)

transit.m: Metrovía BRT (Troncal 1) from a nearby stop to downtown/Malecón, ~30-40 min
Official fixed-zone airport taxi to the city center (~15-25 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; mid-range and upscale restaurants often add a 10% service charge, and rounding up or leaving a little extra for good service is appreciated.
